statements.wave-optics: Wave optics is the branch of optics that considers the behavior of light when it exhibits wave characteristics, particularly when it interacts with objects not much larger than its wavelength, such as a narrow slit. Only waves explain effects such as the colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick.
statements.interference-is-the-hallmark-of-a-wave: A ray passing through slits would continue straight ahead, while a wave spreads out and forms a pattern of bright and dark regions by interference. Such a pattern is the most certain indication that something is a wave, whether water, sound, light or even matter.
statements.wavelength-in-a-medium: When light enters a medium its speed drops to $c/n$ but its frequency stays fixed, so its wavelength shrinks by the same factor: $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$.
statements.huygens-principle: Huygens's principle states that every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself. The new wavefront is a line tangent to all of the wavelets. This one construction explains reflection, refraction and diffraction.
statements.diffraction: Diffraction is the bending of a wave around the edges of an opening or an obstacle. Sound fills a room through an open door while light casts a sharp shadow of the doorway, because the amount of bending depends on the ratio of the wavelength to the opening.
statements.coherent-sources: Coherent waves are in phase or have a definite phase relationship, and they produce a steady pattern of interference. Incoherent waves have random phase relationships and produce none, as with the two headlights of a car.
statements.youngs-double-slit: In 1801 Thomas Young sent light through two narrow slits and found a pattern of many bright and dark lines rather than two lines. The waves from the two slits overlap and interfere, and the experiment gave definitive proof of the wave character of light.
statements.path-length-difference: For a distant screen the paths from two slits a distance $d$ apart are nearly parallel, and the difference in their lengths to a point at angle $\theta$ is $\Delta l = d\sin\theta$.
statements.double-slit-constructive: Bright fringes of a double slit appear where the path length difference is an integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. The smaller the slit separation, the larger the angle of each fringe.
statements.double-slit-destructive: Dark fringes of a double slit appear where the path length difference is a half-integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = (m + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$, so that crest meets trough.
statements.order-of-interference: The order of an interference fringe is the integer $m$ in the conditions for constructive and destructive interference, the number of whole wavelengths by which its two paths differ. The central fringe is of order zero.
statements.find-wavelength-from-a-pattern: Interference patterns measure wavelength: solving $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for whichever quantity is unknown gives a wavelength from a measured angle, or a slit separation from a known wavelength.
statements.highest-order: Because $\sin\theta$ can be no larger than one, setting $\sin\theta = 1$ in the interference condition gives the largest order that reaches the screen.
statements.fringe-spacing: For small angles the fringes of a double slit are evenly spaced on a screen a distance $x$ away, with spacing $\Delta y = x\lambda/d$, which grows with the distance to the screen and the wavelength and shrinks with the slit separation.
statements.diffraction-grating: A diffraction grating is a large number of evenly spaced parallel slits. It forms bright regions at the same angles as a double slit, and gratings work by transmission and by reflection. Opals, butterfly wings and bird feathers owe their colors to natural gratings.
statements.grating-constructive-condition: Each ray from a grating travels $d\sin\theta$ farther than its neighbor, so all of them arrive in phase when $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, the same condition as for a double slit. The slits of a grating are closer, giving fewer maxima at larger angles.
statements.grating-maxima-are-sharper: The bright regions of a grating are narrower and brighter, and its dark regions darker, than those of a double slit. The more slits there are, the sharper the maxima, which is why a grating can separate wavelengths that lie close together.
statements.grating-spectrum-on-a-screen: White light through a grating is spread into a rainbow in every order except the central one, with violet nearest the center. Find the angle of each wavelength from $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ and then its position on the screen from $y = x\tan\theta$.
statements.single-slit-minima: A single slit of width $D$ has a minimum where the rays from its top and bottom differ in path by a whole number of wavelengths, $D\sin\theta = m\lambda$, since each ray from one half of the slit then has a partner from the other half that cancels it. There is no minimum of order zero.
statements.rayleigh-criterion: By the Rayleigh criterion, two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one lies on the first minimum of the other. For a circular aperture of diameter $D$ this occurs at $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$ in radians, so a larger aperture or a shorter wavelength resolves finer detail.
statements.find-a-resolvable-separation: Once the smallest resolvable angle is known, the distance between two objects that can just be told apart is that angle times their distance away, $s = r\theta$.
statements.diffraction-spreading-of-a-beam: Even a beam of rays made as parallel as possible spreads out at an angle of about $1.22\lambda/D$ because its diameter is limited. The spreading can be reduced only by making the beam wider, which is why a laser sent to the Moon is first expanded through a telescope.
statements.resolving-power-of-a-lens: The resolving power of a lens is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as distinct. The Rayleigh angle with the small angle approximation gives it as $x = 1.22\lambda d/D$, and the smaller it is, the greater the resolution.
statements.resolution-and-numerical-aperture: A lens with a larger numerical aperture collects more light, gives a brighter image and resolves finer detail: its resolving power is $x = 0.61\lambda n/\text{NA}$. A larger numerical aperture also makes the focal spot smaller, which in wave optics is never a true point.
statements.thin-film-interference: Thin film interference is the interference between light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a thin film. The ray that enters the film travels farther and may return in or out of phase with the ray reflected at the top, so different thicknesses favor different colors, as in a soap bubble or an oil slick.
statements.phase-change-on-reflection: Light reflecting from a medium with a greater index of refraction than the one it travels in undergoes a 180° phase change, a shift of $\lambda/2$. Light reflecting from a medium of smaller index undergoes none.
statements.thin-film-conditions: For light incident perpendicularly, the ray reflected from the bottom of a film travels about $2t$ farther, measured in wavelengths in the film. Combine that path difference with the phase changes at the two surfaces: a total shift of a whole number of wavelengths is constructive, and a half-integral number is destructive.
statements.nonreflective-coating: A thin layer on a lens can make the light reflected from its two surfaces cancel. When both reflections carry a phase change, the thinnest such coating is a quarter of the wavelength in the film thick, $t = (\lambda/n_2)/4$.
statements.light-polarization: Polarization is the attribute that the oscillations of a wave have a definite direction relative to its direction of propagation. Light is a transverse wave, and polarized light has its electric and magnetic field oscillations in a definite direction. Only a transverse wave can be polarized.
statements.polarizing-filters: A polarizing filter passes only the component of the electric field parallel to its axis, so the light leaving it is polarized. Two filters with crossed axes pass nothing at all.
statements.malus-law: A polarizing filter passes only the component $E\cos\theta$ of a polarized wave's field, and since intensity goes as the square of the amplitude, the transmitted intensity is $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of polarization and the axis of the filter.
statements.polarization-by-reflection: Light reflected from water or glass is partly polarized, more horizontally than vertically, because the vertically polarized part is preferentially refracted. Polaroid sunglasses with vertical axes therefore cut glare.
statements.brewsters-law: Brewster's law states that the reflected light is completely polarized when the angle of reflection is Brewster's angle, $\tan\theta_{\text{b}} = n_2/n_1$, where $n_1$ is the index of the medium in which the incident and reflected light travel and $n_2$ the index of the medium that reflects it.
statements.polarization-by-scattering: Sunlight shakes the electrons of air molecules perpendicular to its direction of travel, and they radiate like small antennae, so light scattered at right angles to the original ray is polarized. This is why the blue sky grows bright and dim through rotating polarizing sunglasses.
statements.optical-activity: Some materials act on the direction of polarization itself. A liquid crystal rotates it by 90° unless a voltage is applied, which is how a pixel of an LCD works; optically active substances such as sugar water rotate it; stressed plastic shows colored patterns between crossed filters; and a birefringent crystal splits a beam in two.
statements.wavelength-limits-microscopy: Because light diffracts around small objects, no microscope using light can show details much smaller than its wavelength. Shorter wavelengths, as in ultraviolet microscopes, show finer detail.
statements.contrast-by-interference: Light passing through an object of different index emerges out of phase with light from the background, and superimposing the two makes the difference visible as contrast. Interference microscopes and phase-contrast microscopes enhance the contrast of nearly transparent objects in this way.

new.name: The axis of a polarizing filter
new.statement: The axis of a polarizing filter is the direction along which the filter passes the electric field of an electromagnetic wave.

new.name: Direction of polarization
new.statement: The direction of polarization of an electromagnetic wave is defined to be the direction parallel to its electric field.

new.name: Horizontally and vertically polarized light
new.statement: Light is horizontally polarized when its oscillations are in a horizontal plane, and vertically polarized when they are in a vertical plane.

new.name: Unpolarized light
new.statement: Unpolarized light is made of waves that are randomly polarized, with every direction of polarization. The Sun and most other sources produce unpolarized light.

new.name: Brewster's angle, $\theta_{\text{b}}$
new.statement: Brewster's angle is the angle of reflection at which the reflected light is completely polarized, $\theta_{\text{b}} = \tan^{-1}(n_2/n_1)$.

new.name: Optically active substances
new.statement: An optically active substance rotates the plane of polarization of light passing through it. Sugar water is an example, and the amount of rotation measures its concentration.

new.name: Birefringence
new.statement: A birefringent crystal splits an unpolarized beam of light into two beams, which are polarized in different directions.

new.name: Contrast
new.statement: Contrast is the difference in intensity between objects and the background on which they are observed.

new.name: The polarization microscope
new.statement: A polarization microscope enhances contrast by using the polarization of light, which makes it useful for objects that are optically active.

new.name: The ultraviolet microscope
new.statement: An ultraviolet microscope is built with special lenses that transmit ultraviolet rays, and it records its images by photographic or electronic means. Its shorter wavelength shows finer detail than visible light can.

new.name: Coherent light
new.statement: Waves are coherent when they are in phase or have a definite phase relationship.

new.name: Incoherent light
new.statement: Waves are incoherent when they have random phase relationships.

new.name: Reflected light that is completely polarized
new.statement: Reflected light is completely polarized when it is reflected at Brewster's angle $\theta_{\text{b}}$.

new.name: Interference microscope
new.statement: An interference microscope enhances the contrast between objects and background by superimposing a reference beam of light upon the light emerging from the sample.

new.name: Phase-contrast microscope
new.statement: A phase-contrast microscope uses wave interference and differences in phase to enhance contrast.
